segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Today was supposed to be Thanksgiving.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You remembered waking up thinking about mashed potatoes, pumpkin pie, and watching football with your family. You remembered the desert air being cool and dry, like it always was in November in Arizona.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You definitely did not expect this.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You press your forehead against the glass of your bedroom window. Outside, towering Saguaro cacti look like giant green snowmen, shivering under three feet of heavy, freezing snow. Icicles hang from the telephone wires like glittering fangs.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And down on the sidewalk, marching in perfect, stiff-legged unison, are soldiers.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Not real soldiers. They are made of polished, painted wood. They wear bright red coats with gold buttons, tall black fuzzy hats, and giant white grins that never, ever close. Their wooden jaws click with every step:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When you went downstairs this morning, your family wasn’t in the kitchen cooking turkey. They were gathered around a glittering, twelve-foot pine tree that definitely hadn't been there yesterday. They were singing carols with wide, glassy eyes, humming along to music that seemed to be drifting out of the floorboards.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When you asked your mom what happened to Thanksgiving, she just smiled a strange, faraway smile.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Thanksgiving? Don't be silly, sweetheart. It’s Christmas morning. It’s always been Christmas morning.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Something inside your chest twisted. You knew—with total, stubborn certainty—that yesterday was Wednesday, November twenty-seventh. But nobody else seemed to remember yesterday at all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the wooden soldiers knocked on your front door.
